note: ru: mod10=1, mod100≠11 ⇒ one. Forms are one|few|many.
mod100=11 is the exception to 'one' ⇒ many.
mod100=12 is the exception to 'few' ⇒ many.
0 ⇒ many (East Slavic).
Negative counts are abs()-normalized: -1 ⇒ one.
sr: BCS shares the East-Slavic integer rule. Forms one|few|other; `sat` is used because all three buckets differ (1 sat / 2 sata / 5 sati).
mod100=11 is the exception to "one" ⇒ other.
mod100=12 is the exception to "few" ⇒ other.
0 ⇒ other, as in East Slavic.
Negative counts are abs()-normalized: -1 ⇒ one.
Script subtag is not part of plural grammar: sr-Latn normalises to sr.
Same rule, Cyrillic script. sr-Cyrl normalises to sr — the script lives only in the author's form text.
hr shares the BCS rule.
bs shares the BCS rule.
101: mod10=1, mod100=1 ⇒ one. Guards the rule past two digits.
111: mod10=1 but mod100=11 ⇒ other. The 11-trap survives past 100.
Region suffix with an underscore also normalises to sr.
Explicit EN locale (2-form). n=1 ⇒ one. (Omitted-locale defaulting to EN is a TS-only contract, unit-tested, not cross-engine corpus.)
EN-style: only n=1 is 'one'; 0 ⇒ many.
Empty count slot ⇒ entire construct erased to ''.
Unsubstituted %n% is non-numeric ⇒ erased to ''.
Truthy = set AND has a non-whitespace char; '   ' is falsy.
'0' is a non-whitespace char ⇒ TRUTHY (a classic gotcha).
No else branch; falsy ⇒ empty string.
Conditional name lookup is case-insensitive (like %var%).
A context value containing %b% expands recursively (up to MAX_VARIABLE_DEPTH).
An unresolved %var% is left verbatim at render time (a warning at validate time, not an error).

A #set on its OWN line INSIDE an enumeration is extracted GLOBALLY (like extract_set_directives), so %x% in the other option sees it. rng:last picks the %x% option ⇒ 'A'. Regression for the directive-global-pass gap.

A #set is a macro: the value is substituted at each %x% and its enumeration re-rolls. Two draws are consumed — seq[0]=0 then seq[1]=1 — which is the observable difference from #def below. A first-option RNG could NOT tell the two apart.
Same template and the SAME rng sequence as set/macro-re-rolls-at-every-reference. A #def is rendered once and frozen, so one draw is consumed and seq[1] is never reached.

Roll-once is not bracket-specific: a permutation freezes too, so both references shuffle identically. Its #set twin below shares the template and the rng sequence and shuffles twice — the pair is the pin, neither half means much alone.
The roll runs AFTER the context is merged, so a definition can read a runtime variable. Rolling it earlier (where collapse-once sat) would freeze the literal text %who%.
Runtime beats every local, #def included; the definition is then never rolled at all.

%b% never mentions %a%: it reaches it through the macro %s%, expanded at reference time and therefore invisible in %b%'s own text. Ordering on direct references alone froze %b% with %a% unexpanded and the plural block vanished for want of a numeric count. Declaration order is deliberately reversed.
Same template and rng sequence as def/rolled-once-covers-permutations; a macro re-shuffles at the second reference.

The permutation-config HTML guard, found missing in a port (spintax-js#58): a leading
  • is HTML, not config, when the tag shape matches AND its closing
    • appears later in the body — the elements keep their markup. Without the guard the whole first tag becomes the single-separator config and the output is mangled markup. rng 'first' reverses a two-element shuffle, hence two before one.

The guard's other half: no anywhere after, so
  • is NOT HTML — it is a config, and a config with none of the four known keys is the single-separator form (the whole string becomes sep AND lastsep). A purely-alphabetic separator is space-padded on join, which is why the output reads 'two li one', not 'twolione'.
A self-closing tag needs no later closer to be HTML — the trailing slash alone passes the guard.

The renderer's guard accepts attributes:
  • …
    • is HTML and renders literally. The VALIDATOR disagrees on this same template — see validate/perm-config-html-with-attributes-is-flagged; the two fixtures together pin the family-wide split exactly as all three engines ship it.

The key-form test is `\b(?:minsize|maxsize|sep|lastsep)\s*=` — a word boundary AND an equals sign, not a substring scan. 'separator' contains 'sep' but is no key, so the whole string is the single-separator form and pads like any alphabetic sep. A substring detector flips this into key-form-with-all-defaults and the word silently vanishes from the output (spintax-js#58, the Pascal port's Pos() test).

The word-boundary half of the same rule: 'xminsize=2' carries minsize= as a SUBSTRING but not at a boundary, so it is no key-form — the whole string is the separator (not purely alphabetic, so it glues bare). A substring detector does worse than default here: it finds 'minsize' inside the word, parses '=2', and renders a genuine minsize-2 permutation. The validator flags this template — validate/perm-config-embedded-key-is-flagged pins that half.

Render twin of validate/directive-check-cr-survivor-satisfies: the parser's four-terminator anchors let '#set %x% = A' sit between a CR and a LF, so it is consumed as a real directive; the malformed head keeps its CR and stays text.

Two definitions of one name: the LAST wins (Map overwrite), so %x% renders B. First-wins resolution renders the self-referential first value instead. The verdict side (definition.duplicate-name) is pinned in validate.

Last-wins turns %a% into a mutual cycle with %b%, and render stays lenient (#57): the 51-hop budget starts at %a%, its parity leaves %b% as the unresolved literal. First-wins resolution renders 'plain' and never meets the cycle.

Render twin of validate/permutation-key-without-equals-is-not-a-key: 'maxsize 2' without '=' is not a key, maxsize stays null, and all three elements render. An extractor with an optional '=' renders a 2-element subset here.

The \s* around a config '=' is the full JS class: a LINE FEED between 'maxsize' and '=1' still parses, so exactly one element renders. Skipping only space and tab reads maxsize as null and renders all three.

The closing '>' scan is QUOTE-AWARE (findConfigEnd): an unterminated quote swallows every later '>', no config end is found, and the '<…>' text falls through into the first element of a default-separator permutation. An engine that reads the config anyway invents a separator or a maxsize the reference never saw.

SEP_RE has NO word boundary — only a (?<!last) lookbehind — so once key form is chosen (the standalone sep="-" satisfies the \b gate), the FIRST sep= match wins even inside 'xsep', and the separator is '.'. Asymmetric with the \b in the key-form gate, and pinned as-is: an engine that requires a boundary in the extractor too picks '-'.

A conditional reaching the COUNT slot resolves before the numeric test, so the block renders. Every engine used to expand variables into the slot and stop there: the conditional survived, failed the numeric test, and the block was ERASED while validate() reported nothing -- and plural.count-macro exempts conditionals precisely BECAUSE they resolve before plurals.
The other branch of the same shape: both are resolved, not just the one that happens to be second.
A branch may hold another conditional; the count slot resolves them all the way down.
Truthiness in the count slot is the ordinary rule, inversion included -- an undefined name is falsy, so {?!missing? takes the then-branch.

NEGATIVE control for the case above. Only conditionals resolve early; enumerations run AFTER plurals, so an enum in the count slot still reaches the numeric test intact and erases the block. Resolving the branch by rendering it instead of substituting it would spin this to 1 and invent a count no engine has.
NEGATIVE control: resolving the conditional is not the same as accepting the result. A branch that is not a number still erases the block.
NEGATIVE control: the slot is tested whole. A resolved conditional surrounded by text is not numeric.

The lenient fallback prints the count as the plural stage saw it -- resolved. Pins WHERE the resolution happens (before every check, not just before the numeric test), which is what makes the fallback text comparable across engines.

The casino-platform report (0.7.0): a runtime %L% = a|b|c|d inside [<…>%L%] is FOUR elements, not one. The plugin expands variables before it reads a bracket, so a | inside a value separates elements; a tree-walk engine has to splice the value as text and re-read the construct. pick = random_int(3,3) short-circuits (no draw); Fisher-Yates with j=0 every step: [a,b,c,d] → i=3 ⇒ [d,b,c,a] → i=2 ⇒ [c,b,d,a] → i=1 ⇒ [b,c,d,a]; take 3.
Same body; j=i every step ⇒ no swap ⇒ the first three in source order.

The production shape: a #set macro wraps the permutation and the list arrives at render time. The macro is re-parsed at its reference, and the construct it holds splices the list like any other. The stripped directive line leaves a leading newline.
[a|%L%|b] with L = x|y is four elements in source order; last ⇒ no swap.
{%L%} with L = x|y|z is a three-way pick, not the literal list; last ⇒ z.
{a|%L%} with L = x|y is three options and index 1 is the first spliced one. One construct, one draw — order-independent by construction.

Plugin Stage 6a resolves {?…} BEFORE expansion, so the taken branch lands in the body ahead of the split: [{?flag?%L%|none}|c] ⇒ [%L%|c] ⇒ [x|y|c]. Both PHP corpus runners run the full Pipeline order (bare Parser::process() has no conditional stage and would give "none c"). last ⇒ no swap.
A #def holding the permutation is rolled ONCE — the only two draws happen during the roll — and the held text is reused at both references; the list inside it is spliced like anywhere else.
The <config> is text to the plugin too: sep="%S%" takes its value before the permutation is read, so the re-read has to start from the config again. last ⇒ no swap.

A per-element separator is text to the plugin as much as the config is: `a <%S%> | b` takes the separator from the value before the elements are read. last ⇒ no swap; a non-alphabetic separator is not padded.
lastsep="%S%" takes its value like sep does; an alphabetic separator is space-padded on join. last ⇒ no swap.

The hop budget is the reference's 51 inside a bracket as at top level (render/circular-set-accumulates-then-stops is the top-level pin). Fifty aliases and a terminal list: the 51st pass puts `x|y` INTO the body before the enumeration is read, so it is two options (last ⇒ y). An engine that hands the last hop back as finished text renders `x|y`; one that spends a 52nd hop differs on the next case.

The plural slots run the same fixpoint: fifty aliases into `1` reach the number on the 51st pass and the block renders. A slot that stops at 50 sees `%a51%`, non-numeric, and erases the block (spintax-js 0.7.0, found in review).

Fifty-one aliases into END: the 51 passes leave `%a52%` in the form list, and the reference never expands again — the picked form is that literal. An engine that re-expands the picked form after its slot pass renders END (spintax-js 0.7.0, found in review).
NEGATIVE — the guard on the rule: with no construct around it, a | in a value is text.
NEGATIVE — an undefined name is left literal and is ONE element, exactly as before.
NEGATIVE for the outer construct: the list inside {%L%} belongs to that enumeration (last ⇒ y); the permutation around it still has two elements. Order-independent under last.
#set %x% = {p|q}|r is spliced as text: the enumeration resolves in place (last ⇒ q) and r becomes its own element ⇒ three elements, no swap.

The reported preset (minsize=5;maxsize=7, sep ", ", lastsep " and ") over an eight-name runtime list. The size pick is the FIRST draw — random_int(5,7) ⇒ 6 — then Fisher-Yates i=7..1 with j=0 each rotates left by one ⇒ [B,C,D,E,F,G,H,A]; take 6.

expect.output: B, C, D, E, F and G

note: Truthy is /\S/u in the plugin, and /u is PCRE2_UCP: U+FEFF is not whitespace there, so a value of U+FEFF alone is set and non-blank. JavaScript's \s counts U+FEFF as whitespace.
The mirror of conditional/bom-only-is-truthy: U+0085 (NEL) is \s under UCP and not in JavaScript's \s, so a value of NEL alone is blank.

The config patterns carry NO /u in PHP — byte mode, ASCII \s — so a no-break space around '=' is not config whitespace: no key matches and the whole string is a single separator. The ASCII twin is perm/config-ascii-ws-around-equals. JavaScript's \s is Unicode on any flags, which made this a minsize of 1.

A reference in a size key is text to the reference engines — expansion runs over the whole text before the config is read — so minsize=%n% IS a size: one element of three. 0.7.0 marked a permutation only on its PARSED separators, where %n% never arrives (a size that is not digits parses to nothing), and rendered all three (#80).

An UNQUOTED sep=%S% whose value carries the quotes: after expansion the config reads sep=", ", so the separator is ', '. 0.7.0 parsed the unquoted form to the default separator before any value existed and never marked the construct (#80). The quoted form is splice/config-separator-from-variable.

Stage 6a resolves {?…} before any bracket is read, so the taken branch 'b|x' lands in the body and its pipe separates elements: three elements, no '|' in the output. 0.7.0 marked a conditional only when a %var% sat in its branches, rendered 'b|x' as ONE element and printed the pipe (#80).
The same for {…}: the taken branch 'b|x' becomes two options, so the enumeration has three and 'last' picks 'x'. 0.7.0 had two options and printed 'b|x'.

The ordinary authoring shape: a list item gated by a flag. With the flag unset the branch is empty, the plugin's element split drops the empty part, and the list is two items. 0.7.0 kept the blank element, so the separators around it survived — 'Есть покер, слоты и.' in a real template (#80).
The plugin trims each element after Stage 6a, so whitespace at the edge of a taken branch is the element's edge and goes. 0.7.0 rendered the branch as it was written, spaces and all.

NEGATIVE, guarding what #80 must not move: a conditional whose taken branch has no '|', no blank and no edge whitespace re-reads to the tree it already was, and every draw — both nested enumerations, then the shuffle — lands exactly where 0.7.0 put it. A re-read that shifted RNG order would re-roll content hosts have already published.

The plugin resolves enumerations (Stage 7) before permutations (Stage 8), so when {live casino|} picks its empty option the permutation splits 'slots||poker' and drops the empty part. A tree walk renders the elements first: 0.7.0 kept the blank one and printed 'slots, , poker' (#80, found by differential against both PHP engines).
The same order trims: { a |b} picks ' a ', and the plugin trims each part it splits, so the element is 'a'. 0.7.0 joined the padded text.

The size pick counts the elements that remain: with {b|} empty there are two, so minsize=3;maxsize=3 clamps to 2 and the render is two elements with one separator. 0.7.0 counted three and joined an empty one — 'a  c'.

A {?…} inside a per-element separator is text to Stage 6a like one in an element, so '<{?g?, |; }>' is '<; >' before the split. The first cut of #80 marked a construct only for a conditional IN AN ELEMENT, and printed the raw conditional here unless a neighbour happened to trigger the re-read (found in review).
The same in the <config>: lastsep="{?en? and | и }" with en unset is lastsep=" и " by the time the plugin reads the config.

An element dropped because it renders empty takes the per-element separator it carried with it: the plugin drops the part AND the separator pending for it, so 'a<1>|{x|}|b' joins as 'a b'. Keeping the separator, or handing it to the next element, prints 'a1 b'.
The separator written AFTER a dropped element still belongs to the next one: in 'a<1>|{x|}<2>|b' the empty part drops with the '1' it was given, and 'b' keeps the '2' — 'a2b'.

NEGATIVE for an engine that keeps variables in a JavaScript object: `constructor` and `__proto__` match \w+ and are ordinary names, undefined here, so both stay literal — both PHP engines read variables from arrays. @spintax/core 0.7.0 found Object's own members under them: this template threw TypeError out of render(), and %__proto__% rendered as nothing. A reference is lower-cased before the lookup, so %CONSTRUCTOR% reached them too.
`{?…}` on a name nothing defines is falsy whatever the name. 0.7.0 read Object and Object.prototype under these two and took both then-branches, and neither inverted one.
A #set may define either name. Assigning `__proto__` on a JavaScript object changes the prototype instead of storing a value, so 0.7.0 lost that definition and rendered the reference as nothing.

Runtime context keys are names like any other, `__proto__` included — a JSON-decoded context carries it as an ordinary key. 0.7.0 dropped it while merging the context, so the reference rendered empty.
def/rolled-once-and-held under a prototype name: one draw, held for both references, seq[1] never reached. 0.7.0 lost the rolled value the way it lost a #set, and printed "-".

Definitions are rolled in the order of the names their values reach through macro values. 0.7.0 looked those names up in a plain object, found Object's members under `constructor` and `__proto__`, and threw TypeError reading them as text. Undefined, both stay literal.

A runtime list under `__proto__` is spliced as text like any direct reference (#78): three elements, shuffled. 0.7.0 dropped the key and read Object.prototype instead, whose text '[object Object]' then parsed as a permutation of its own.
An undefined name in a form slot stays literal and the block resolves. 0.7.0 substituted Object.prototype's '[object Object]', and its brackets sent the block to the fullwidth fallback.
ar (#88): six forms in CLDR order zero|one|two|few|many|other. 0 ⇒ zero. The forms are bucket labels so a wrong pick names itself.
n%100 = 0 ⇒ other: the bucket the two-form rule never had.
n%100 = 2, but only n = 2 itself is "two" — 102 is other.
n%100 = 3 ⇒ few again, above 100.
A negative count uses abs(), as every locale does.
The same rule over a real noun, كتاب (book), from #88.
A two-form block under ar is the arity mismatch every locale has: fullwidth fallback, no silent English rule.
#87: a letter-only separator is space-padded, unless every letter is Han, Hiragana or Katakana — scripts written without spaces between words. last ⇒ no swap.
#87: Hiragana joins bare too.
#87: ー (U+30FC) is Script=Common, but it is written inside Katakana words, so it belongs to the unpadded set.
#87: Hangul keeps the padding — Korean puts spaces between words.
#87: a separator that mixes scripts keeps the padding. Letters only on purpose: and/和 is not letter-only and was never padded at all.
#84: the name class is [A-Za-z0-9_]+, so a digits-only name is an ordinary name. PHP coerced the array key to an int and lost the rolled value.
#84: the rolled value reaches a later definition under the same name.
#84: two digits-only names in a chain. PHP printed a fragment fifty times here before 0.9.0, because the name it wrote and the name it read were different keys.
#84: the macro half.
#84 controls: 0 and 07. PHP only coerces a canonical integer key, so 07 was always fine and 0 too — pinned so a fix cannot break them.
#88: 101 is other. n%100 = 1, but only n = 1 itself is "one" — an engine that tests n%100 === 1 picks one here.
#87: halfwidth Katakana with the halfwidth prolonged-sound mark U+FF70, which is Script=Common like U+30FC and belongs to the unpadded set for the same reason.
#90: under ar, the conjunction و (and ف) is written attached to the next word — a space before it, none after. last ⇒ no swap.
#90: the author's spaces around و change nothing, as they never changed the padding: ' و ' and ' و' join like 'و'.
#90: ف ("and then") is a proclitic like و.
#90: the rule is keyed by the BASE language — ar_SA and ar-EG are ar.
#90: و attaches only before a letter of the Arabic script. Before a Latin brand the space stays, as Arabic typesetting writes it.
#90: a digit is not a letter, Arabic-Indic digits included — the space stays. Decided, not derived: the rule attaches before a letter only.
#90: the next element is read by CODE POINT. U+1EE00 (Arabic mathematical alef) is an astral letter of the Arabic script; an engine reading one UTF-16 unit would see a surrogate and pad.
#90: أو ("or") is a word of its own, not a proclitic — padded as before.
#90: Persian writes the same letter و as a separate word, with spaces — the rule is keyed by language, not script.
#90: Urdu likewise — the proclitic rule is ar and he only.
#90: with no locale the engine cannot know the language — و is padded as before.
#90: Hebrew ו ("and") is a proclitic like Arabic و.
#90: או ("or") is a word of its own — padded as before.
#90: Thai is written without spaces between words, like Han and kana (#87) — a letter-only Thai separator joins bare.

expect.output: แมวและสุนัข

note: #90: Lao, like Thai.
#90: the issue's real path — an Arabic comma for the inner separators, و before the last, the default post-process on.

#87/#90: the unspaced test reads Script. U+3006 (〆) is Script=Common with Han only in its Script_Extensions, so it is padded like any other letter. PCRE2 10.40+ reads \p{Han} as Script_Extensions and would join it bare.
#90: the next element is tested for a letter of Script=Arabic. U+0640 (tatweel) is Script=Common with Arabic only in its Script_Extensions, so و keeps both spaces before it.
#90: Khmer, like Thai — a letter-only Khmer separator (U+1780) joins bare. Most Khmer words carry a combining mark and were never padded; this pins the script itself.
#90: Myanmar, like Thai — a letter-only Myanmar separator (U+1000) joins bare.
#90: ו attaches only before a letter of the Hebrew script; before a Latin word both spaces stay.
